articles.title: A hidden risk appears to be building up in the markets. No one knows exactly what it means
articles.summary: If you look only at the obvious numbers, you wouldn’t ever see it.
articles.body: If you look only at the obvious numbers, you wouldn’t ever see it. But an estimate of potential risk that’s hidden to all but the most attentive investors and economists has been building up in the bond market for months. It’s called the term premium, and it just hit a 12-year high. No one knows precisely why the wonky metric seems to be saying it’s riskier now to invest for the long haul than it was during the inflation crisis, the global trade war or the pandemic. But it’s got one corner of investors sweating. It could be nothing but noise. It could reflect nervous energy among investors. Or it could signal that the bond market is pricing in even more economic danger than people realize. The term premium Here’s what’s going on. (And don’t worry, we’ll hold your hand through some seriously nerdy stuff.) If you’re an investor who wants to buy Treasuries over the course of the next 10 years, you have multiple options available to you. For example, you could buy a 10-year bond. Or you could buy a 5-year bond and roll it over halfway through the decade. Or you could buy a 2-year bond and roll your investment over five times. You get the picture. In a perfect world, the cost of buying a long-term bond should be the same as rolling over short-term bonds in the same time period. A decade is a decade no matter how you slice it. The risk is the same. But we don’t live in a perfect world; we live in a cloud of uncertainty. Right now, investors have put a significant premium on buying 10-year Treasuries compared to short-term bonds that roll over multiple times throughout the next decade. The term premium estimates the value of that extra charge. According to two models, it hasn’t been this high since the spring of 2014. Still confused? Think of it this way. Let’s say you have a hungry kindergartner. You give her a candy bar and tell her: “I want you to wait 10 minutes before you eat this. I’ll be back to check on you.” The likelihood that the kid is going to chow down is probably higher if you leave her alone for 10 whole minutes than if you check in on her every two minutes. But the term premium can be negative, too, as it was throughout the pandemic and as recently as two years ago. In that case, the kindergartner isn’t hungry – she’s spiteful. She’s more likely to eat the candy if you keep tabs on her every two minutes than trust her to hang on to it for 10 minutes. The near-term risk is higher than over the long haul. Right now, the market appears to be telling us that the kindergartner is ravenous and investing for the next 10 years could come with some considerable risk. What it means Now, the even trickier part is understanding why the term premium is suddenly so high. Certainly, there’s a ton of risk in the marketplace. Investors are uncertain about AI, ballooning debt, the Iran war, geopolitical uncertainty… but the past 12 years were pretty bananas, too: Is it really less safe to invest over the next decade than at any point since 2014? Market analysts and economists note the term premium is poorly understood and subject to interpretation. Among the possibilities: It’s riskier to invest now: The simplest interpretation is that long-term investing really is riskier now than in the past. AI spending is measured in the trillions of dollars, and the rapidly developing technology is reshaping the economy in ways that are difficult to predict or understand. The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday said rising government debt across the world is becoming unsustainable. Populist economic policies have found favor on the left and the right, and neither spending reductions nor higher taxes have much support among most major economies. The Iran war has reignited worldwide inflation without a clear endgame, and President Donald Trump left open the possibility of resuming US attacks on Iran after the midterms. Central banks around the world would probably respond to even higher fuel prices by raising interest rates. All those factors are sending bond yields to multi-decade highs, raising the cost of borrowing and threatening to slow economic growth. But inflation from AI and fuel shortages may not slow down even if the economy cools off, potentially complicating the government’s ability to intervene with emergency action if necessary. And one unpredictable dynamic that could throw a wrench in the economy’s gears: shifting geopolitics. France may elect its first far-right president since World War II. The UK’s welfare state is crumbling. The Middle East is a powder keg. China and the United States are engaged in a high-stakes battle for AI supremacy. And US midterms could yield unpredictable results in November. “It’s important that economists like myself and other capital markets professionals remain humble about our own Achilles heel: its geopolitics,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US. “We get it mostly wrong, our models and metrics rarely capture those dynamics and are often behind the curve when things get kinetic.” Investors think it’s riskier to invest now: But the term premium doesn’t necessarily measure actual risk. It could measure the perception of risk for investors. “Don’t infer because there’s a higher risk premium, there’s higher risk,” said Thierry Wizman, economist at Macquarie Group. “It could just be that people are more averse to risk.” Like a gambler riding a hot streak, investors staring at record-high stock prices and a fast-growing economy may become nervous that their luck is about to run out. Economic conditions haven’t really changed all that much recently: Unsustainable debt loads have been a problem for decades. AI growth has been on a massive upward trajectory for years. Inflation has been above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target for five years. But something may be rattling investors, and they’re looking for insurance to park their money over the long haul. “Prices look calm, but people are quietly buying insurance everywhere,” said Nigel Green, CEO of DeVere Group. “Typically, when everyone’s nervous but prices haven’t moved, things don’t adjust gently if the bad news comes; they lurch.” The model is wrong: It’s also possible that the model isn’t saying what we think it is. The recent rise in the term premium may have nothing to do with Iran, AI or debt at all. It could be explained by technical factors. For example, large funds may have been rebalancing their portfolios at the end of the third quarter. “Because the term premium represents the component of a bond yield that cannot be explained by the expected path of short-term interest rates, it is difficult to identify precisely what drives it,” noted Neil Shearing, economist at Capital Economics. So the best we can do is guess – and proceed with caution.

articles.title: China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
articles.summary: Sanctions and a North Korean leadership that prioritises security dim prospects for trade, analysts say.
articles.body:
As China and North Korea cut the ribbon on New Yalu River Bridge this week, officials described the new border crossing in momentous terms.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the 3km (1.9-mile) bridge, which links China’s Dandong and North Korea’s Sinuiju, would “vigorously promote” trade and “strengthen emotional bonds”.

North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song expressed his belief that the crossing would “accelerate the advance for the prosperity of the two countries” and “add fresh vigour” to their economic cooperation.

Analysts on China-North Korea ties are much more circumspect.

While the bridge is a concrete symbol of China and North Korea’s efforts to revitalise relations that have waned from their Cold War-era peak, the prospects for trade are hindered by obstacles ranging from international sanctions to a North Korean leadership that prioritises security above all else, experts say.

“It reflects China’s renewed effort to strengthen its relationship with North Korea at a time of changing regional alignments,” Phillip Park, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, South Korea, told Al Jazeera.

“But whether this leads to substantially deeper economic integration, greater North Korean dependence, or a significant shift in Pyongyang’s strategic orientation remains an open question.

“The bridge could facilitate trade and logistics, but it does not remove international sanctions,” Park added.

China, whose troops fought alongside Pyongyang in the 1950-53 Korean War, has long been North Korea’s most crucial economic benefactor.

China accounts for as much as 95 percent of official trade with the secretive country, which is among the world’s most diplomatically and economically isolated states.

Before the four-lane New Yalu River Bridge officially opened on Thursday, road and rail freight between Dandong and Sinuiju, the main route for China-North Korea trade, travelled exclusively via the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge.

Opened in 1943, the bridge, which has a single-lane road and a rail track, can only carry vehicles weighing a maximum of 20 tonnes.

Jae-woo Joo, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, said the new bridge could “tremendously” boost trade between the sides, including the transfer of components banned under sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes.

“It is therefore really significant to open this bridge with China,” Joo told Al Jazeera.

After coming under strain from North Korea’s nuclear weapons tests in the mid-2000s, Beijing-Pyongyang ties have warmed under Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

At Xi and Kim’s most recent meeting in June, their seventh summit since 2018, the leaders pledged to enhance cooperation in areas spanning trade, defence, agriculture, law, science and technology.

Analysts have, in part, cast Beijing’s deepening engagement with Pyongyang as a response to the latter’s growing ties with Moscow, which have included the deployment of thousands of North Korean troops to the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Last month, North Korean and Russian officials opened the first road bridge linking their countries across the Tumen River.

North Korea and China’s two-way trade grew 25 percent in 2025 to reach $2.74bn, according to figures from China’s General Administration of Customs.

Bilateral trade has continued to grow in 2026, jumping nearly 20 percent to reach $1.5bn in the first half of the year, putting it on track to reach its highest volumes since the COVID-19 pandemic.

But while growing, trade remains relatively minuscule in the context of global commerce.

With China’s overall trade hitting $6.36 trillion in 2025, North Korea’s contribution to the total was a little more than 0.04 percent.

Official trade between the neighbours also remains substantially below its 2010s heyday.

Trade hovered around $5-6bn throughout much of the decade, peaking at $6.45bn in 2013.

Economists have offered explanations for the slowdown that range from tightened sanctions to China’s waning reliance on imports amid its efforts to boost economic self-reliance.

Christopher Green, a senior consultant for the Korean Peninsula at International Crisis Group, said the new border crossing’s significance should not be overstated, considering that China-North Korea trade “is fundamentally driven by politics”.

“Lack of cross-border transit routes is not the main obstacle,” Green told Al Jazeera.

“If the bridge opening signifies a political desire on both sides to give political cover to rising trade volumes, then a boost to trade should follow,” Green said, describing ties up until now as “steady-as-she-goes” economic engagement.

“Time will tell. But the key is the politics of national security, not economics.”

As much as officials have hailed the New Yalu River Bridge as a reflection of Chinese-North Korean cooperation, the project had a long and torturous road to completion.

Construction began in 2011 and was finished on the Chinese side in 2014.

But North Korean authorities only completed roads and customs facilities on their side of the river this year following repeated pauses in construction amid tensions with Beijing.

“The 12-year delay certainly suggests that economic cooperation is more conditional than the language of friendship might imply,” Marco Mari, a PhD researcher at Bocconi University in Italy who studies China-North Korea economic ties, told Al Jazeera.

“The bridge can facilitate supplies and economic activity, while Russian support gives North Korea alternatives that diminish Beijing’s leverage,” Mari added.

“This does not necessarily imply broader economic reform or a comparable improvement in ordinary people’s lives.”

Weiqi Zhang, an associate professor at Suffolk University who studies relations between North Korea and China, said the history of China-North Korea economic ties is littered with abortive projects, such as the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone, a North Korean-Chinese development near Dandong.

“There were cases, like the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone – established by China and North Korea – where China built infrastructure on its side, but North Korea didn’t even pave the road on their side,” Zhang told Al Jazeera.

“One reason is that, unlike its neighbours, North Korean government doesn’t really pay much attention to trade for economic development,” Zhang said.

“International trade is used by North Korea more like a foreign policy tool.”

With China wishing to demonstrate its “indispensability” as a trade partner and North Korea eager to strengthen their economic ties, trade is likely to grow, said Edward Howell, a lecturer in international Relations at the University of Oxford.

Even so, economic engagement will be subject to political considerations, Howell said.

“North Korea will obviously want to avoid facing any Chinese influence to change its economic model, but Pyongyang will want to reap the economic benefits of trade with its principal economic benefactor,” Howell told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Memory stocks slide into another bear market as chip losses near $2.5 trillion: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) entered another bear market this week, falling more than 20% from its September rebound high.
articles.body:
AI's appetite for memory keeps growing while investors' appetite for memory stocks is shrinking.

The Roundhill Memory ETF ( DRAM ) entered another bear market this week, falling more than 20% from its September rebound high. Losses deepened Thursday, leaving the fund roughly 22% below that peak and nearly 40% below June's record close.

It's been an expensive round trip. DRAM plunged nearly 45% from June to late July, then rallied over 40% into September. The latest selling has erased more than three-quarters of that recovery.

Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ), Micron ( MU ), SK Hynix ( SKHY ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ) — all DRAM components — have shed more than $700 billion in combined market value since October 6. A broader Yahoo Finance basket of 61 semiconductor and storage stocks has lost nearly $2.5 trillion.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% Thursday in Seoul, before US trading began. The subsequent US rebound helped Micron finish nearly 2% higher, but the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) still posted its eighth straight decline — its longest losing streak since October 2008.

Strong demand hasn't stopped investors from questioning future profits.

China's CXMT ( 688825.SS ) has announced progress on a denser memory-chip design , raising concerns about competition and pricing power. Yet the challenger fell, too — over 5% Thursday, leaving it down roughly 20% since September's end. DRAM holds it as well, with roughly 5% exposure as of September 30.

Meanwhile, chipmakers helping finance their customers are attracting more scrutiny. That doesn't mean AI demand has disappeared. TSMC ( TSM ) reported another record quarterly profit Thursday. Investors are questioning how much of the boom will reach shareholders.

DRAM's next major test sits around its late-July lows near $45 — another 9% below Thursday's close. Holding there would preserve the summer trading range. A sustained break would erase the rebound entirely.

articles.title: Investors — and Elon Musk — crashed CoreWeave stock. But many analysts don't see the problem.
articles.summary: Even as investors are fleeing, some analysts see a well-positioned neocloud.
articles.body:
It's been a rough few days for CoreWeave ( CRWV ) investors. Shares of the neocloud provider plummeted 15% on Wednesday and are down around 25% in the past week and a half.

The sell-off was ostensibly fueled by a widely circulated chart that illustrated rising borrowing costs , which was amplified by Elon Musk on X with a one-word damning response: "yikes."

The reaction was so intense that CEO Mike Intrator sent an internal memo to staff saying that the market was acting "irrationally."

The metaphorical Fed chair of AI financing, Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, also spoke up in CoreWeave's defense , highlighting his own entangled interests with a partner company and the urgency within the industry to keep sentiment bullish on the AI build-out.

But even as many investors are fleeing, multiple big-name Wall Street analysts don't see alarm bells — and agree with Intrator. Bank of America analysts — who, let's remember, are held to a high standard of objectivity — reiterated their Buy rating and a price target of $140 on Thursday, more than double the share price of current trading.

Analyst Tal Liani wrote in a note on Thursday that CoreWeave's track record gives confidence. "We believe CoreWeave's greatest competitive advantage is its ability to bring active power online at scale," he said, adding that the company's risks are controlled in multiple ways.

Rather than build data centers, CoreWeave primarily leases data center capacity "from a diversified set of third-party developers," Liani wrote. The company signs both sides of its deals between infrastructure providers and customers simultaneously and uses up-front cash and the reputations of blue-chip customers to reduce borrowing risk.

The structure of contracts also supports predictable financing and a clearer view of its bookings, Liani wrote. While other neocloud companies use shorter-term contracts for higher prices, CoreWeave primarily sells capacity through five-year contracts to large hyperscalers and AI labs. That locks in a lower cost of capital, Liani said, and provides a high degree of revenue visibility.

Analysts at Deutsche Bank are also clinging to an optimistic view of CoreWeave, expressing confusion and surprise at the investor panic. Brad Zelnick wrote in a note on Thursday that the sell-off presents a buying opportunity.

"We struggle to find company specific factors that justify the recent move, and the fundamental market backdrop for AI infrastructure remains quite supportive based on the signals we see," he said.

articles.title: Car shoppers have had it with price increases
articles.summary: Affordability is the key constraint facing car dealerships.
articles.body:
More car buyers are exercising their most powerful negotiating tool: walking away.

It probably has something to do with the idea of an $800 car payment , the painful result of near-record prices for new vehicles and stubbornly high interest rates.

Affordability is the key constraint facing publicly traded dealerships, according to Bank of America analysts led by Alexander Perry, in a note on Thursday. In parts and service too, customers are pushing back on pricing and putting off repair work.

Ahead of earnings, BofA is lowering earnings estimates on five major dealers, including Asbury ( ABG ), AutoNation ( AN ), and Group 1 ( GPI ), because of weaker demand for new units and more deferrals on recommended work.

The average transaction price for a new vehicle is now above $50,000, according to a recent analysis by Kelley Blue Book. And it's not just because Americans love their trucks and large SUVs. Two of the most popular, more affordable segments are also driving up the average price. Price increases on subcompact SUVs and compact cars means there is no escape from car inflation.

BofA's survey of 70 dealers found that vehicle pricing was the most cited constraint on new vehicle sales, at 66%. Financing costs came in as the second most popular reason, at 47%. Inflation and high interest rates, clear as day.

More than half of the dealers reported seeing some pushback on pricing as customers delayed work. And another 11% of dealers said they are losing repair orders altogether as customers balk at the cost.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title: Job-switching used to be one of the best defenses against inflation. That advantage is disappearing
articles.summary: In years past, when Shannon Ratcliff switched jobs, she often got more than career advancement — she got a nice little pay bump.
articles.body: In years past, when Shannon Ratcliff switched jobs, she often got more than career advancement — she got a nice little pay bump. But this year, her new job came with a $20,000 pay cut. The job is a great opportunity, she said, and she’s hoping to advance and close that financial gap. However, the salary drop-off is still tough to stomach for her family of five at a time when prices are rising faster than normal. “Everything is getting more expensive, but the amount of money we bring home is less and less,” she said. The US labor market has lost some of its oomph, leaving workers like Ratcliff with less leverage to boost their income and keep pace with inflation: the pay premium for switching jobs. Pair that with five years of stubborn inflation, and workers are losing even more ground. In September, the median increase in base pay for job changers was 4.8% versus 3% for job stayers, according to data from payroll giant ADP. That gap has not surpassed 2 percentage points for nearly two years. For context, it was north of 7 percentage points during the post-pandemic jobs boom and sat comfortably above 3.5 percentage points pre-pandemic. “Switching a job gives you a one-time burst, but it still is not enough to keep up long term with inflation at the levels we’re seeing now,” said Nela Richardson, chief economist at ADP. Last month, overall inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index rose at an annual rate of 3.7%. Job switchers aren’t seeing their pay gains completely eroded by inflation, but they don’t have the breathing room that they once did (pre-pandemic, that difference was roughly 5 percentage points). Stifled hiring Dynamism is an important ingredient in a healthy labor market (and healthy economy, for that matter). The ability for employees to find the best opportunities for themselves and for employers to find the best candidates for the job help to drive innovation, which drives productivity, which drives growth, Richardson has said. But instead, the labor market has been in a period of relative stasis, turnover data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows. The hires rate (hiring as a percentage of total employment), an indicator of labor demand, has plodded along at decade-low levels, excluding the pandemic. The quits rate, which represents workers’ confidence in their ability to find a new job, remains near a six-year low. Job growth last year was one of the weakest on record. Employment gains have picked up this year, with the economy adding 68,000 per month versus fewer than 10,000 per month in 2025. However, they remain well below historical averages, BLS data shows. Hiring has been stunted by a combination of factors including pervasive uncertainty, a shrinking labor supply, higher oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty, stubborn inflation, rising borrowing costs, and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence technologies. That has left workers increasingly worried about their job security: In September, Glassdoor’s Employee Confidence Index fell to a new record low – its third such nadir in 2026 for the 10-year-old index. The bottom-barrel sentiment also reflects a buildup of workers having to endure six years filled with crises, including a global pandemic, Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor said at the time of the report’s release in late September. Navigating the ‘I’m not sure what is going to happen’ economy The process of switching jobs has never been a costless endeavor, Richardson said. “You have to update your resume; you’ve got to get on a [job posting site]; you’ve got to do multiple interviews, which may mean taking personal days,” Richardson said. “But particularly in a low-hire, low-fire labor market, it takes longer when employers are being selective.” That’s especially true when the labor market waters are choppy. “Is a 2% (pay bump) worth it for all the other stuff you have to do to get onboarded? Is 3% worth it?,” she said. “You can certainly say 16% is worth it, but there’s got to be a de minimis in which ‘I might just stay where I am in this slightly volatile, I’m not sure what’s going to happen’ economy. Sticking with the same employer seems to be what people are generally doing.” Shannon Ratcliff’s job search took six months and six days – roughly the national average, BLS data shows – after being laid off in early December last year. Having little luck in getting interviews for finance and accounting positions, Ratcliff pivoted to human resources and obtained certifications in the process, which helped her land the role she has today. For Jorena Collins, a senior technical writer in Colorado, a “brutal” nine-month job hunt ended with a contract position that pays about half of what she made two years ago. “I’ve built a career from nothing twice now, but the market isn’t what it was; and it’s honestly been very discouraging,” she wrote to CNN in response to a callout on job-switching. For her first career, Collins had worked her way through college to obtain a degree in physics that afforded her opportunities as an engineer. After stepping away from the workforce to raise her children, the gap limited her engineering opportunities, and so she rebuilt her career as a technical writer. “I worked my way up through some of the biggest names in tech and eventually earned more than I ever had as an engineer,” she wrote. “That was a couple of years ago. Now with AI taking on more of the technical writing, it’s been difficult to find work.” In a follow-up phone interview, Collins talked further about the toll taken. “The last nine months have been just nerve-wracking,” she said, as some emotion hit her voice. During that time, some medical bills had accumulated, and she’s now in a place where she’s making too much for Medicaid but not enough for insurance. She said she’s grateful for the position she’s found, especially as her field – and many others – is being reshaped by the adoption of AI, yet another force that job seekers have to contend with when looking for new roles. Collins, who uses AI in her personal and work environments, said she sees great potential from it but added that the technology needs more governance and guardrails to protect against any dangers as well as to handle the fallout of job loss. “I think the whole world is going to be in the same position. I think I’m being affected first. I think we’ll get better at switching (jobs) as the world changes – and adapting,” she said. “But right now, it’s difficult to try and guess what job might last a few years before AI takes over.”

articles.title: Rs 10,000 crore for small businesses: Who can benefit from India's new SME Growth Fund?
articles.summary: The Union Cabinet’s approval of a Rs 10,000-crore SME Growth Fund has opened a new route to equity financing for growth-oriented small and medium
articles.body: The Union Cabinet’s approval of a Rs 10,000-crore SME Growth Fund has opened a new route to equity financing for growth-oriented small and medium enterprises (SMEs), with manufacturing businesses set to receive the bulk of investments.But for business owners, the key questions are whether their enterprises qualify, how they can access the capital and what conditions will govern the investments. Unlike a bank loan or government grant, equity financing involves giving investors an ownership stake or other equity rights in a business.The Cabinet approved the government’s commitment of Rs 10,000 crore towards establishing the SME Growth Fund on October 6, following its announcement in the Union Budget 2026-27 on February 1.According to the finance ministry’s Cabinet release, the fund is intended to provide direct equity investments to enterprises with demonstrated business viability and the potential to scale up.The government says the initiative is intended to address a gap in growth capital for SMEs. Existing equity-support mechanisms have largely focused on early-stage businesses and micro enterprises, leaving some established companies struggling to secure the long-term capital required for expansion, technology adoption and entry into international markets.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced the proposal in her Budget speech, saying, “I propose to introduce a dedicated ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund, to create future Champions, incentivizing enterprises based on select criteria.”The announcement made growth capital a central part of the government's push to help promising enterprises expand.What is the SME Growth Fund?The fund is designed to provide what the government describes as patient equity capital to high-potential SMEs. According to the official PIB factsheet issued on October 6, the investment vehicle will support enterprises across manufacturing, services, technology, innovation-driven sectors and strategic value chains.A major share of the fund’s allocations will go to manufacturing-focused SMEs. Businesses operating in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities will also be considered, according to the Cabinet announcement. The government expects the investment to help businesses expand their operations, improve productivity and become more competitive.The fund will operate through an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF). In practical terms, this means the government’s commitment will be channelled through an investment vehicle that makes equity investments in selected companies, rather than being distributed as a fixed cash grant to every eligible business.This distinction matters because equity financing is different from a conventional business loan. A loan generally requires repayment of the principal and interest under agreed terms, whereas equity investment involves an ownership interest or other agreed equity rights in a business.Equity can help companies finance expansion without the same scheduled debt repayments, but it may also dilute existing ownership and involve investor rights.For instance, if a company receives Rs 2 crore in exchange for a 10% ownership stake, it gains capital without taking a conventional loan, but its existing owners give up part of their ownership. This is only an illustration, not a confirmed investment structure under the fund.The Cabinet announcement does not specify the final commercial terms for individual investments. Valuation, ownership stakes and exit arrangements will therefore need to be established through the fund’s operational framework.Who can benefit from the fund?The revised MSME classification, effective April 1, 2025, provides the starting point for understanding which businesses fall into the small and medium categories.According to the MSME ministry’s official classification, a small enterprise has investment in plant and machinery or equipment of up to Rs 25 crore and annual turnover of up to Rs 100 crore. A medium enterprise has investment of up to Rs 125 crore and annual turnover of up to Rs 500 crore. Both limits apply together.However, falling within these thresholds does not automatically qualify a business for investment from the SME Growth Fund. The government has described the intended beneficiaries as enterprises with demonstrated viability and scalability, and the Budget refers to incentivising businesses based on selected criteria.Manufacturing businesses are the clearest priority group. A company seeking to expand production capacity, modernise machinery or develop new manufacturing capabilities could fit the stated objectives.Technology-led enterprises, businesses developing innovative products and firms seeking to enter export markets may also fall within the fund’s broad scope. These are examples of businesses that align with the stated objectives, not guaranteed beneficiary categories.The government has additionally identified enterprises in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities for consideration. This could broaden the geographical reach of growth capital, although the Cabinet announcement does not establish a fixed allocation for particular cities or regions.The distinction between classification and selection is important. The MSME thresholds establish whether a business falls within the small or medium category; they do not establish that the business will receive investment. The final selection criteria will determine which enterprises are chosen.Why does growth-stage equity matter?The fund is aimed at businesses that have moved beyond the earliest stages of development but need substantial capital to expand. While bank loans remain important for working capital and investment, additional debt may not always be the most suitable way to finance long-term expansion.The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) welcomed the Cabinet decision in a statement issued on October 8. The industry body said the fund could support enterprises across manufacturing, technology, innovation-driven sectors and strategic value chains.The statement also described the initiative as having the potential to create India’s own “Mittelstand of globally competitive manufacturing enterprises”.The reference to the Mittelstand, Germany’s network of competitive small and medium-sized businesses, reflects the ambition to help Indian enterprises grow into globally competitive companies rather than remain small suppliers.The economic rationale is that companies seeking to expand production, enter new markets or adopt advanced technology may require capital before those investments generate returns. Equity can provide risk capital without the same scheduled principal repayments associated with conventional borrowing, although its suitability depends on a company’s prospects and the commercial terms offered.The government’s broader policy rationale is also reflected in the Economic Survey 2025-26, which examines MSMEs’ contribution to manufacturing, exports and employment. The government’s SME Growth Fund factsheet cites the Survey’s estimate that MSMEs account for 31.1% of GDP, 35.4% of manufacturing output and 48.58% of exports.These figures underline the sector’s economic importance, but the new fund targets a narrower group of growth-oriented small and medium enterprises. Its impact will depend on whether it reaches businesses with credible expansion plans and whether investments translate into higher productivity, greater manufacturing capacity and stronger export competitiveness.How can businesses access the money, and what remains unclear?The government has announced the broad investment structure, but the practical route for companies seeking funding is yet to be fully detailed.The finance ministry’s Cabinet release confirms that the government will commit Rs 10,000 crore towards establishing the SME Growth Fund for direct equity investments. The PIB factsheet explains the intended beneficiaries and broad investment framework.However, the official documents reviewed do not provide a complete public application procedure, a confirmed date for applications to open or minimum and maximum investment amounts for individual companies.For prospective beneficiaries, the questions are straightforward: Will companies apply directly or approach an investment manager? What financial records and business plans will be required? How will investment proposals be evaluated, and what commercial terms will apply?The identity and role of the implementing and investment-management authorities also need to be established through official notices.Until the implementing authority publishes or confirms these details, businesses should not assume that meeting the MSME classification criteria is sufficient to secure investment. Nor should the fund be treated as a grant that can be claimed automatically.A business seeking equity investment generally needs to demonstrate a credible growth strategy, financial viability and the ability to use the capital productively. These are common considerations in equity financing, but the fund’s specific requirements must be confirmed through its formal framework rather than assumed.Another issue is the relationship between the fund’s aggregate commitment and its annual Budget provision. The Union Budget’s Notes on Demands for Grants for 2026-27 lists Rs 500 crore for the SME Growth Fund in the Budget Estimates, while the Cabinet has approved an aggregate commitment of Rs 10,000 crore.The two figures represent different funding measures and should not be treated as contradictory. The Budget provision is for a particular financial year, whereas the Cabinet announcement refers to the aggregate commitment. The documents cited do not establish the complete contribution schedule or when the first investments will reach businesses.The distinction between growth equity and broader MSME credit support is also important. The government announced the SME Growth Fund alongside other measures in the Union Budget 2026-27, including an additional Rs 2,000 crore for the Self-Reliant India Fund to continue risk-capital support for micro enterprises. These are separate initiatives with different intended roles.The broader policy challenge is whether equity investment can help established firms overcome the capital constraints that prevent them from expanding. The fund could help selected companies scale up, but it is not designed to meet the financing needs of every small business.For business owners, the immediate takeaway is that the Rs 10,000-crore commitment signals a dedicated push towards growth equity, particularly for manufacturing-focused SMEs. But the amount committed to the fund is not the same as money already invested in companies.The fund’s success will ultimately be measured not by its headline size alone, but by whether it helps promising enterprises expand capacity, adopt technology, improve productivity and become more competitive. For now, the immediate question is when the investment process will begin and which businesses will be able to access it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: BofA’s Hartnett Sees Investors Avoiding Risk on Fed, Midterms
articles.summary: Risk aversion is set to dominate markets in coming weeks as investors seek shelter from higher interest rates and volatility around US midterm elections and...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Risk aversion is set to dominate markets in coming weeks as investors seek shelter from higher interest rates and volatility around US midterm elections and the AI trade, according to Bank of America Corp.'s Michael Hartnett.

A summer of "extreme bull sentiment" has come to an end, while the broad selloff in global bonds has driven yields adjusted for inflation to 3%, the strategist said in a note. Higher energy prices and sticky inflation are also adding to investors' list of worries.

"We continue to lean risk-off next 3-4 weeks given 3% real yields," Hartnett wrote. He said his team expects an October rate hike by the Federal Reserve "to restore credibility" after inflation ran above the central bank's target for more than five years. He also sees rising chances of a "wave-like" Democratic sweep in the November midterms.

The BofA strategist's call for a rate hike, published in a note on Oct. 15, is more hawkish than broad market pricing. Swaps traders pared bets on an increase on Friday after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month.

Investors have become increasingly concerned about whether the massive investment in AI infrastructure, and the borrowing to fund it, will be justified. Bets on the AI trade have powered the rally in US stocks, with technology funds attracting record annualized inflows of $196 billion in 2026, the BofA team said, citing figures from EPFR Global.

Hartnett said his team favored adding exposure to "peak yield" beneficiaries in small caps, real estate investment trusts and the consumer discretionary sector. "We don't add tech."

articles.title: What happens if AI agents start speaking their own language?
articles.summary: Humans’ ability to check up on AI agents depends on being able to communicate in a shared language.
articles.body: Part of Chris Painter’s job is to help figure out what happened when AI goes rogue, then publish the results in public reports. He and METR, the nonprofit AI research group he helps lead, have been busy lately: They helped OpenAI untangle the Hugging Face hack this year, and Painter recently testified in front of a Senate subcommittee following a string of other rogue AI incidents. Researchers at METR pore over AI agents’ scratch pads – the “chain of thought” data that can help humans see the steps bots took before responding to a request. That information was key in METR’s investigation of the Hugging Face incident. But Painter is worried that job could soon get a lot harder. Humans’ ability to check up on AI agents depends on being able to communicate the way the bots communicate, in a shared language. What happens if we stop speaking the same language? Or what if AI agents stop showing their work entirely? “If they’re becoming less monitorable, then they have more opportunity to kind of do things that we don’t intend,” Painter told CNN last month. Understanding how AI models think Many AI models — and the AI agents they power — use a method known as “chain-of-thought reasoning” that outlines their process for completing a task. Chain of thought reasoning breaks down processes into a logical sequence of steps, which can help AI models arrive at more accurate answers. For researchers, chain-of-thought data can provide clues to what went wrong. If an AI agent goes rogue and breaks into other systems, researchers can see whether the chain-of-thought data included mentions of deceitful actions, like hacking. METR examined roughly 1,300 raw chain-of-thought transcripts during its investigation into the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. Painter expressed concern that paper trail may one day become unintelligible if AI models begin using their own language to track their steps. “If that were to happen, then like when an investigator goes in, they’ll look around and it’ll all just be numbers everywhere,” he said. AI models could use shorthand references, similar to how a human would when transcribing notes, that are intended for the model to understand so that it can work faster, according to Mark Riedl, an artificial intelligence professor and director of the machine learning lab at the Georgia Institute of Technology. But much like most humans when looking at shorthand, it would probably look like gibberish. There are a few theories for how the chain-of-thought process works, but researchers aren’t sure which ones are correct, says Jacob Andreas, an associate professor at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. An AI model may also decide the best way to meet the criteria it was trained for, like using less power or taking fewer steps, involves producing a chain-of-thought that doesn’t look like legible English. That’s just one concern — another is that models are getting better at executing tasks without even logging their chain of thought. Riedl said newer models can reach the same conclusions without producing a traceable chain-of-thought. While companies can train their models to produce a chain of thought, doing so is more expensive and slower than having the model process tasks internally. OpenAI found that its monitoring systems would be less likely to detect when its new Astra model behaves in undesirable ways through chain-of-thought compared to older models, according to documentation from early September. It also found that Astra could accomplish more tasks without using chain-of-thought reasoning and that it was more capable of controlling its chain of thought. The company wrote that it would lose confidence in its current systems’ ability to detect misaligned behavior – that is, when models take unsanctioned steps that don’t align with human values – if that trend continues. Jakub Pachocki, chief scientist at OpenAI, wrote in a September blog post that AI was getting better “manipulating its own reasoning process” and that models are becoming “smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all.” OpenAI said in a statement last week that it’s investing “significant resources” in the ability to monitor AI models. This came after the company fired three safety and alignment researchers, though OpenAI said the dismissals were not tied to employees voicing safety concerns. In its Astra-related documentation, OpenAI said it’s investigating why the model is more capable of controlling its chain-of-thought, along with methods for protecting against potential misalignment that could be caused by a lack of chain-of-thought. OpenAI pointed CNN to its Astra documentation and Pachocki’s post when asked why Astra is less monitorable and whether the company plans to make future models more monitorable. Trying to understanding AI under the hood The other challenge is that chain of thought doesn’t provide the full picture of why AI models make certain decisions. Complex tasks can require multiple agents generating thousands of words worth of logs outlining their steps, which could feel like trying to monitor a thousand people talking out loud, Riedl said. While AI could help summarize those texts, there’s been some evidence that suggests AI omits important details, he added. Chain-of-thought data shows what an AI model did before arriving at an answer or taking an action but doesn’t reveal why. Humans can control the data and parameters that AI models are trained on, but they don’t understand how these factors may influence the way models behave. It’s possible to look for patterns in an AI model’s neural network – a computational model often used in AI that’s meant to resemble the human brain – but it’s difficult to prescribe precise meaning to those patterns, said Andreas. Anthropic published a research paper in July indicating that it had found small collections of neural patterns within Claude associated with certain words. Still, that doesn’t mean Claude is saying that word. “I think we’re still very far from being able to claim that we have any sort of fine-grained understanding of how the model is actually arriving at a solution,” MIT’s Andreas said. AI’s rapid advancement makes this issue all the more pressing to Painter. With AI increasingly being used in AI research, he worries that information may come out faster than people are able to process it. But he also thinks the Hugging Face saga has cast a spotlight on concerns about rogue AI that have been prominent among AI researchers for years. “I think it has been heartening,” he said. “It really feels like people, when they were talking about this a long time ago, were underestimating how much help there would be from the whole world when the whole world is paying attention.”

articles.title: The US economy is facing two hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House
articles.summary: The wars in Iran and Ukraine are heating up at a bad moment for the US economy and the White House.
articles.body:
Yields are above multi-decade highs , both gas and diesel prices continue to climb , and critical midterm elections are around the corner.

Adding to pressure on the US economy and the current administration, the world's two largest hot wars are heating up.

In the Middle East, dual fronts along the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea have seen a resurgence of conflict in recent weeks that heavily disrupted oil flows in the region.

Multiple tankers and container ships in the Strait of Hormuz either caught fire or sank this week in the Iran-dominated waterway. The Washington Institute has tracked more than two dozen attacks recorded since the start of the month.

President Trump has said the US military won't resume airstrikes inside Iran before the midterm elections as White House negotiators continue angling for a diplomatic solution to the conflict now in its eight month.

At the same time, administration officials are reportedly war-gaming a major offensive to come after the November elections, when the president will be less encumbered by the political needs of the Republican Party.

"The Trump Administration does not want Brent crude oil at $106/bbl going into the midterm elections, just a month away, and has said that he only plans to escalate offenses against Iran after the midterms are over, with what he hopes to be, a red wave," Rabobank cross-asset macro strategist Molly Schwartz said in a recent note to clients.

To the west along the Red Sea, Yemen's Houthi militants have sharply escalated their campaign against Saudi coalition opposing the group's bid for wider territorial control, launching multiple rounds of strikes on major airports inside the kingdom that have killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds.

Houthi militants recently struck an office building belonging to the state-managed oil giant Saudi Aramco ( 2223.SR ). While the kingdom's oil production remains largely undisrupted, violent pestering by the Iran-allied Houthis is driving up oil prices .

"Iran knows when the midterms are too," Schwartz added, "and if they want to further complicate Trump's plans, now is the perfect time to have the Houthis stir up trouble and make it increasingly difficult for the US to avoid intervening."

Ukraine, Russia, and Starlink throttling

Ukraine and Russia, which have been at war since Russia executed a stealth annexation of Crimea in 2014 and invaded its neighbor in February 2022, recently both escalated offensive strikes against critical infrastructure ahead of another winter.

articles.title: Truist shares edge down on revenue miss despite earnings beat

articles.body:
Investing.com -- On Friday, Truist Financial Corp. (NYSE:TFC) reported third quarter adjusted earnings per share of $1.16, beating analyst estimates of $1.14.

The Charlotte-based bank's stock declined 2.53% in pre-market trading following the results.

Revenue came in at $3.79 billion on a taxable-equivalent basis, and fell short of the $5.35 billion consensus.

The bank posted adjusted net income available to common shareholders of $1.42 billion for the quarter ended September 30, up 12% from $1.35 billion in the prior year period. However, reported revenue of $3.75 billion missed expectations, impacted by a $1.45 billion loss on the sale of available-for-sale securities and a $66 million loss related to the Regional Acceptance Corporation loan sale. Excluding these items, adjusted revenue was $5.30 billion, down 0.1% from the second quarter.

Net interest income on a taxable-equivalent basis increased 1.1% to $3.71 billion compared to the prior quarter, while rising 0.7% YoY. The net interest margin expanded two basis points to 3.00%. Revenue declined 27.8% YoY when including the securities losses.

"We delivered a solid quarter while also taking decisive actions to better position Truist for the future," said CEO Mike Lyons. "These actions strengthen our risk, liquidity, and funding profile and create greater capacity to invest in our best businesses."

The bank completed the sale of its Regional Acceptance Corporation loan portfolio during the quarter and signed an agreement on October 14 to sell $7.7 billion of unsecured consumer loans from its LightStream platform to Carlyle Group Inc. Average loans and leases held for investment decreased 1.1% to $325.5 billion, while average deposits increased 1.4% to $410.7 billion.

Asset quality improved following the RAC loan sale, with nonperforming loans declining to 0.40% of total loans from 0.51% in the prior quarter. The net charge-off ratio was 0.77%, which included 39 basis points related to RAC.

articles.title: Tesla Roadster probably won't drive an earnings beat, but the big reveal did achieve 2 things
articles.summary: Elon with a win.
articles.body:
The new Tesla ( TSLA ) Roadster probably won't be the deciding factor in the company beating on earnings when production possibly begins in 2028, but the high-profile reveal on Thursday night did achieve two things.

"Two takeaways from tonight's Roadster event. 1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together," veteran tech analyst Gene Munster said in an X post.

Tesla unveiled its redesigned Roadster on Thursday night at SpaceX's ( SPCX ) rocket test site in McGregor, Texas. It came nearly nine years after Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk first showed his idea for the car in 2017.

Using cold-gas thrusters borrowed from SpaceX and a suction system, the car drove upside down on a curved ramp, vaulted off it, and flipped in midair before landing. The car also jumped over a series of Tesla vehicles — not unlike the classic move of K.I.T.T. from the "Knight Rider" TV series.

Musk said it can reach 60 mph in under a second and top 230 mph, though it is unclear whether any of the stunt features would be legal on public roads.

Tesla said production will start in 2028. There is a $50,000 deposit on the Performance version and $250,000 on the Thrust version.

Tesla stock rose 5% in premarket trading on Friday, while SpaceX advanced 2%.

"Wait who the hell was driving the Tesla," Meta ( META ) AI chief Alexandr Wang said on X of the flying Roadster.

"We are pleased to report excellent third quarter results," said Alan Schnitzer, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. "It was another in a run of successful quarters, with very strong underwriting performance across all three segments and a record result from our investment portfolio."

The company reported a consolidated combined ratio of 86.8%, improving from 87.3% in the prior-year quarter, while the underlying combined ratio was 84.1%. Net favorable prior-year reserve development totaled $234 million pre-tax across all three segments, though this included a $295 million addition to asbestos reserves.

Net written premiums reached $11.480 billion, essentially flat YoY. Excluding the impact of divested Canadian operations, premiums grew 2%. Business Insurance premiums increased 4% on an adjusted basis to $5.868 billion, while Bond & Specialty Insurance grew 12% to $1.209 billion. Personal Insurance premiums declined 7% to $4.403 billion, or 3% excluding the Canadian divestiture.

Net investment income hit a record $1.098 billion pre-tax, up 6% from the prior-year quarter, benefiting from higher yields and growth in average invested assets.

articles.title: Why are consumers so negative on a good economy? It’s the inflation, stupid.
articles.summary: Republicans are frustrated that the public has such a sour view of the economy, especially when growth is accelerating and we may be on the cusp of what some are calling America’s economic “golden age.” Rising prices are the ongoing problem, and the most recent inflation readings did nothing to turn around voters’ gloom. A hotter-then-expected…
articles.body:
Republicans are frustrated that the public has such a sour view of the economy, especially when growth is accelerating and we may be on the cusp of what some are calling America’s economic “golden age.”

Rising prices are the ongoing problem, and the most recent inflation readings did nothing to turn around voters’ gloom. A hotter-then-expected Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index , delivered in recent days, could not have come at a worse time for the Republican Party.

The latest report indicated that inflation, instead of moderating, actually accelerated last month, jumping 0.6 percent month-to-month after rising 0.4 percent in August. More than half the increase, not surprisingly, was from higher energy prices , which rose 5.2 percent from the previous month. Core prices, excluding energy and food, gained 0.3 percent , as they did in August.

Given that Democrats have made affordability the centerpiece of their argument for taking back control of Congress, they seized on the news with glee.

The House Democratic Caucus posted on X , “Trump promised to lower costs and end inflation on day one. The exact opposite has happened. This president has been a total failure.”

Consumer pessimism about the economy, brought on by higher-then-expected inflation, has translated into poor approval ratings for the president and the Republican Party, dimming chances that Republicans will hold onto their majority in the House and the Senate in the midterm elections next month.

That isn’t the norm; typically, Republicans score higher than Democrats on questions like “Who do you trust more to handle the economy?” Not today. A recent Washington Post headline captures the moment: “Democrats hold big edge on economy in key poll for first time since 2012.” The Post writes, “A majority of adults, 51 percent, chose Democrats when asked, ‘Which political party do you think will do a better job of keeping the country prosperous?’ A smaller group, 37 percent, selected Republicans.”

The sentiment shift is frustrating because, in many ways, it doesn’t make sense. America’s banks recently reported mainly strong earnings . But the most noteworthy information delivered from our nation’s banks was that the consumer is doing extremely well.

JPMorgan reported that credit and debit card sales volume was up 10 percent over last year. Wells Fargo’s release cited an incredible 12 percent gain in credit card charges , and an 8 percent jump in debit card spending. Not left behind was Citigroup, where card spending soared 13 percent.

Those are extraordinary numbers for a population recording the lowest confidence numbers in 12 years. And no, the spending surge was not boosted solely because of higher gasoline prices, though that had an impact. Nor were rising outlays financed by mounting debt. In fact, JP Morgan actually dropped the rate of charge-off’s on consumer credit card debt, indicating that borrowers were keeping up. The other banks also reported improving consumer credit quality.

How could this be? According to Wells Fargo’s CEO, consumers are spending because strong employment and wage growth have helped Americans absorb higher prices. Jane Fraser, CEO of Citi, said much the same : “The labor market is stable and companies remain active.”

Here’s the disconnect: economic growth, real income gains, low unemployment and other signs of a healthy economy have been buried under a blanket of anxiety about inflation. Certainly, the liberal media and Democrats running for office have amplified the bad news about rising prices and ignored the more positive news.

Making matters worse, Republican candidates appear incredibly inept at delivering the good news. Republicans seem fearful of repeating the error made by President Biden as he prepared to run for a second term: telling Americans they didn’t understand how well off they actually were. Of course, that was as inflation hit a peak of more than 9 percent ; today, the numbers are not nearly so bad, but consumers are dealing with a cumulative price jump of more than 20 percent since COVID hit the nation — most of it occurring on Biden’s watch.

Gerard Baker at The Wall Street Journal voiced his frustration (and touched that third rail of questioning voters’ judgement) in an op-ed titled , “It’s the Economy, Stupid—but How Stupid?” He pointed out that, “As in 1992, Democrats are poised to win big based on mistaken perceptions that times are difficult.” Comparing today to the year that President Clinton was running for president the first time, Baker notes, “But now as then, it may be that a flawed perception of the economy rather than economic reality is driving voting behavior, and that now as then the U.S. is in the early stages of an economic golden age.”

He reminds readers that, “By the time Americans voted that November, the recession Gov. Clinton had rhetorically exploited [in his campaign against Republican George H.W. Bush] was long over . During the second half of 1992, gross domestic product expanded at an annual rate of 4 percent. Unemployment peaked that summer and was falling sharply by the time the new president took office.” It didn’t matter. Clinton sold the public that the economy was in bad shape, and he won.

Today, we are enjoying solid growth, rising real incomes, low unemployment (and continuing claims are very low), stock markets near record high, and an investment boom. Moreover, we may indeed be on the precipice of what Baker calls an economic “golden age” because of the potential gains from artificial intelligence.

Black Rock CEO Larry Fink, also writing in the Journal, voiced similar sentiments , writing that AI “seemed likely to produce tremendous growth. That growth was the answer to America’s economic Achilles’ heel, its federal debt, which has now reached a record $40 trillion. Expanding the economy by more than 3% a year is ultimately how countries meet the promises they have made … AI makes that kind of growth more achievable than it has been in decades.”

How ironic that the public has turned so negative on this potential golden age.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: PepsiCo just lost KFC to Coca-Cola. Here's how much it could sting financially.
articles.summary: This has shaped up to be a year of big losses for beverage and snack giant PepsiCo.
articles.body:
This has shaped up to be a year of big losses for beverage and snack giant PepsiCo ( PEP ).

A double-digit percentage drop in the stock so far this year. Lost sales in the core soda business to rival Coca-Cola ( KO ). Lost profits because of execution missteps and inflation (see the recent full-year earnings guidance cut).

And the losses look to keep piling up, with the latest one being a really tough one to swallow for longtime PepsiCo and Yum! Brands ( YUM ) followers — and probably a legion of former execs, such as former legendary PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi and her equally legendary former counterpart at Yum! Brands, David Novak.

The Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday that Yum! Brands-owned KFC struck a deal with Coca-Cola to be its beverage provider for thousands of US restaurants. The deal will reportedly begin in January. PepsiCo will reportedly still supply KFC internationally.

Note that in April, Coca-Cola won the Marriott ( MAR ) business from PepsiCo.

Yum! Brands spun off from PepsiCo in 1997 under the original name of Tricon Global Restaurants. It changed its name to Yum! Brands in 2002.

The spin-off included PepsiCo's fast food restaurant division: KFC, Pizza Hut, and Taco Bell. The business relationship between the two companies has long been seen as a sacred bond, apparently until now.

"Overall, the move underscores Coca-Cola's strong brand equity as well as a relative brand equity gap vs. PepsiCo," Evercore ISI analyst Robert Ottenstein said. "We believe that this announcement, in some ways, is more notable as QSRs, more so than hotel chains, use beverages as a key driver of traffic."

Ottenstein's analysis shows the lost revenue to PepsiCo could be about $50 million, "which suggests that the retail revenue is closer to ~$350-400 million."

articles.body:
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock fell 5% in premarket trading Friday as concerns over AI funding continued to weigh on investor sentiment.

The decline comes after CoreWeave stock rebounded from a 7% drop on Thursday, following comments from ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang that helped ease concerns over the company's debt-heavy balance sheet.

"CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang shared at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."

A viral chart showing CoreWeave's spiking bond yields earlier this week underscored concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale its business quickly enough to cover rising interest expenses.

Nvidia's backing is significant , given that the AI chip giant holds roughly 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave, representing about a 10% stake in the company.

CoreWeave is also a major customer of Nvidia's chips, underscoring the close ties between the two companies.

CoreWeave was on track to finish the week down 15% as of Thursday's close, following a volatile stretch.

Meanwhile, peer Nebius ( NBIS ) fell 3% in premarket trading, putting it on course for weekly losses as well.

articles.title: Why CoreWeave, Nebius, and other neocloud stocks are being pounded: Goldman Sachs explains
articles.summary: Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.
articles.body:
Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.

CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are both down about 15% just in the past five days.

While concerns about CoreWeave's financial health are being blamed for the neocloud stock routs, the reality is that it's not just a CoreWeave issue. The overall financial health of the AI economic system build-out is being more closely scrutinized in a land of higher-for-longer interest rates.

Goldman Sachs explained the pressure quite well in a new note on Friday.

US dollar high-yield AI-related debt spreads widened by 25 basis points between Oct. 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360 basis points over Treasurys. By contrast, non-AI-related debt spreads were only two basis points wider and remain below their March peak, Goldman Sachs pointed out (see charts below).

Within AI-related debt issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance.

"While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate," Goldman Sachs strategist Amanda Lynam explained. "Further removed AI-adjacent Energy and Utilities have been more resilient, in our view partly reflecting more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile. We think the widening reflects a reassessment of the economics of the AI buildout, particularly for lower-rated borrowers that are more exposed to higher-for-longer rates and potential energy-cost pressures."

Lynam sees "some near-term reversal" of the recent sell-off in US high-yield debt tied to AI. But she acknowledges that "dispersion across AI-related issuers is likely to remain high."

articles.title: Apple iPhone Duo preorders sell out, deliveries extend to late January
articles.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo preorders sell out immediately.
articles.body:
Preorders for Apple's ( AAPL ) $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo sold out in minutes after opening Friday, with delivery dates jumping from Oct. 23 to late January.

Apple's most ambitious iPhone yet, the passport-sized Duo features a 5.4-inch front display and a 7.6-inch foldable inner screen, with a nano-texture finish that helps prevent glare while making the panel's center crease all but invisible.

The book-style foldable is a first for Apple, which has sat out of the folding-phone market for years, leaving rivals Samsung ( 005930.KS ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) to grab market share and iterate on their designs.

But Apple is notorious for letting other companies do the legwork to develop a new market, only to swoop in and grab its own piece of the pie. That's exactly what the iPhone maker did with the AirPods and Apple Watch, which have become bestselling devices in their respective categories.

The iPhone Duo brings a number of new features to Apple's all-important product line, including the ability to run two apps side by side or two windows of the same app simultaneously.

Apps seamlessly transition from the front screen to the main display and back. You can also take advantage of the Duo's foldable design by positioning it like an open laptop on your desk and viewing content on the top of the screen while navigating on the bottom half.

In standing mode, you can position the Duo like a tent on a flat surface to watch shows and movies or use the phone as a high-powered clock for your nightstand.

Apple has also thrown in some extras on the camera. When you unfold the phone and open the camera app, the front screen will provide your subject with a preview of your shot. The idea is to spare friends, couples, and everyone in between the awful experience of having someone take your picture, only to immediately look at the result and demand a redo.

The Duo gets ultrawide-angle and wide-angle rear cameras, but no telephoto option. Up front, the phone gets Apple's Center Stage camera, which helps keep the user in view even if they move side to side.

There's also a FaceTime camera hidden beneath the main folding screen.

Foldable phones are still a relatively niche market segment. According to market research firm IDC , manufacturers were projected to ship 1.25 billion units in 2025. Foldables were expected to make up just 20.6 million of those.

But the company said it anticipates foldable smartphones will account for roughly 10% of the market by 2029. It hit a major cumulative milestone in 2026 with total lifetime units set to surpass 100 million by the end of the year, according to Counterpoint Research's latest Foldable Smartphone Market Forecast .

articles.title: Tesla stock pops after unveiling Roadster with compressed air thrusters for limited flight
articles.summary: Tesla finally unveiled the long-awaited Roadster on Thursday night.
articles.body:
After a two-week delay, the Tesla ( TSLA ) Roadster event went off with a massive bang — a flying one.

The wedge-shaped, cyberpunk-looking Roadster EV appeared in front of an inverted half roller coaster ramp erected at SpaceX's facility in Waco, Texas. The Roadster cruised halfway up — glued to the ramp using a vacuum fan system — then launched off the ramp upside down and performed flips in the air, using air thrusters to right itself and land on the tarmac.

Tesla stock rose as much as 5.4% during premarket trading on Friday following the Roadster event.

Then the Roadster performed a similar stunt, jumping over several Teslas (including a semi), inverted itself, and then used its thrusters to land — an automaker first.

"Well, it worked," CEO Elon Musk deadpanned.

The Roadster also went 0-60 mph in less than 1 second (0.81 seconds) during a test Tesla conducted at the event. While Tesla claimed the car could hit a top speed of 230 mph, Musk boasted that the production version could target half the speed of sound, or Mach 0.5 (383 mph).

So when can you expect to get one? "We enter production in 2028," Musk said.

Tesla said the car comes in three configurations:

Performance: road-ready, seats 2, with multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off track;

Thrust: race-ready, seats 2, with multi-mode suction system and rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable 0–60 in <1 second

Rocket: air-ready, seats 1, with multi-mode suction system, plus perimeter-mounted cold-gas thrusters for forward, upward acceleration and lateral rotational movement. So ... yes, it can fly.

Tesla said the three versions had a range exceeding 300 miles, with a top speed of up to 230 mph for the Rocket version. Officially, in terms of performance, 0- 60 mph across the range is <1.6 seconds for Performance, <0.9 seconds for Thrust, and <0.59 seconds for Rocket.

No word yet on how the Rocket version, with its thrusters that allow short flights, would be allowed on public roads.

The event came two weeks after the initial Oct. 1 reveal date. Tesla said the reveal was pushed back due to weather conditions at the demo site, SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Rocket Development and Testing facility in Waco, Texas .

Tesla is asking prospective buyers to put down a $5,000 deposit, followed by a $45,000 wire transfer due within 10 days of the initial deposit.

Tesla has not said how much the new Roadster will cost, though it is expected to exceed $250,000.

Tesla bull Gene Munster of Deepwater Management had two big takeaways from tonight's Roadster event. "1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring Tesla and SpaceX together," he posted on X.com .

articles.title: Washington Post journalist hospitalized after Israeli settler attack on Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
articles.summary: A Washington Post photojournalist was hospitalized after Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank attacked her and a group of Palestinians during the annual olive harvest.
articles.body: A Washington Post photojournalist was hospitalized after Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank attacked her and a group of Palestinians during the annual olive harvest. Veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was on assignment for the Washington Post, said the group of Palestinians she was with began to retreat when they saw dozens of settlers running toward them. In a video statement, Levine said settlers kicked her while she was on the ground. “I had my camera bag and my pouch with my passport, and my telephone was on a rope around my neck and they broke that off me, and they broke my cameras off me, and they broke my bag, and they kept kicking me,” said Levine, who estimated the attack lasted 10 minutes. “Just absolute craziness, and I didn’t see anybody trying to stop it.” “I don’t know how a parent can raise such a monster. They’re not even humans, and yes, they are Jewish terrorists,” Levine added. “And you know what? Sadly, none of them will be prosecuted. I am sure of it.” The Washington Post said Levine was wearing “visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist” during the attack. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.” Video of the attack showed a group of masked settlers, some armed with clubs, hurling stones at a group of Palestinians, some of whom are also throwing stones. In the background, at least five settlers surround Levine and throw her to the ground, beating her as she covers her face with her hands. The settlers appear to rip away Levine’s bag. The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it was treating two people after they were beaten by settlers: a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man. The assault is part of a wave of settler attacks at the start of the Palestinian olive harvest that residents reported across the area. Last year’s olive harvest saw a surge of such incidents across the West Bank as settlers attacked Palestinians and prevented them from accessing their land. Levine was rushed to the Ramallah Government Hospital after the attack, where she was in stable condition, according to the Foreign Press Association (FPA). Photos show Levine’s hand and leg wrapped in bandages as she rests in a hospital bed. The FPA condemned the attack and called on the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command, which governs operations in the West Bank, to “stop making excuses and do its job of protecting civilians from these violent mobs.” In a statement, the FPA said, “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other cilivians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.” Additional videos from the scene show a man with a bloodied face after the attack, as well as flame pouring out of a burning car with Palestinian license plates. Another video shows Israeli soldiers blocking the road. One soldier films with his phone; a second hurls what appears to be a smoke grenade as a man begs him, “Please don’t do it!” Israel Police opened an investigation after receiving reports of the attack. In a statement, police said they “view any act of violence with great severity, particularly when it involves members of the media carrying out their work.” The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they would examine “all circumstances” around the incident. “Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area,” the IDF said. “Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts.” Mustafa Barghouti, head of the Palestinian National Initiative, said on X that “gangs of Israeli terrorist settlers” launched an attack on the village of Abu Falah, where Palestinians were preparing to harvest their olives. “In full view of the cameras, the settlers set olive trees on fire, pelt Palestinian farmers with stones, and fired live ammunition, resorting to every possible form of terror and intimidation to prevent Palestinians from harvesting their own olive trees,” said Barghouti. This is a developing story and will be updated.
